aspect: EXAMPLE - almost every worker suffers a violation
description: Centro de los Derechos del Migrante's 'Ripe for Reform' found every H-2A worker interviewed suffered at least one serious legal violation, and 94% experienced three or more. 43% of 100 workers surveyed said their pay was less than promised during recruitment in Mexico.
energy_note: Ninety-four per cent, three violations or more.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the debt arrives before the job does
description: Despite recruitment fees being illegal under both US and Mexican law, CDM's 'Recruitment Revealed' found 58% of surveyed workers paid one. At the consulate a State Department official asks whether a fee was paid - by which point many are already deeply in debt because of it.
energy_note: Asked at the window whether he paid the fee he has already paid.

aspect: EXAMPLE - enforcement finds violations almost everywhere it looks
description: Department of Labor investigators in the Southeast region found violations in 78% of more than 280 investigations conducted in 2020.
energy_note: Four in five inspected employers, in breach.

aspect: EXAMPLE - H-2B has even less protection
description: Unlike H-2A, H-2B does not require employers to provide housing or court-enforceable contracts. From 2018 to 2020, 853 H-2B workers were victims of labour trafficking. In Briones v. JNS Construction Services, 69 Mexican citizens sued over forced labour, each having paid a $400 recruitment fee and $250 for travel.
energy_note: Six hundred and fifty dollars, to be trafficked.

aspect: Complaining ends the visa and the next season
description: The worker who reports is not rehired next season, and blacklisting travels between recruiters in the same towns.

aspect: The recruiter is in his own town and known to his family
description: Recruitment happens through local intermediaries in small Mexican towns, so refusing or complaining has consequences at home, not only in the destination country.
energy_note: The man who recruited him drinks with his uncle.
